theory.title: Meaning beyond the literal
theory.explanation: At C2 level, interpretation depends not only on what a speaker says but also on what they choose not to say, how strongly they commit themselves, and what assumptions they expect the listener to supply. Distinguish entailment (what must be true if the statement is true), presupposition (what is treated as already accepted), and implicature (what is suggested in context). Treat any inference as defeasible: context, irony, genre and speaker intention may overturn it.
theory.tip: Before inferring intention, identify the literal proposition, the linguistic cue and at least one plausible alternative reading.

patterns.label: Hedging
patterns.pattern: It would appear that… / Arguably… / To some extent…
examples: It would appear that the figures have been selectively presented.
Arguably, the omission is more telling than the statement.

patterns.label: Concession
examples: Granted, the wording is ambiguous; that does not make every reading equally plausible.

patterns.label: Restricting a claim
patterns.pattern: This is not to say that… / Far from suggesting…, …
examples: This is not to say that the author endorses the policy.

patterns.label: Retrospective inference
examples: The committee may have anticipated the backlash.

items.prompt: The board said the proposal was “not without merit”. What is the most defensible inference?
options: The board sees some value but remains reserved.
The board has rejected it unequivocally.
items.answer: The board sees some value but remains reserved.

content.passage:
When the review panel published its findings, it stopped short of accusing the department of deliberate concealment. Instead, it observed that several omissions were “difficult to reconcile with the stated commitment to transparency”. The phrase was carefully chosen: it neither established intent nor treated the omissions as trivial. Some commentators took it as an implicit allegation; others argued that the panel was merely recording an administrative failing.

The chair subsequently said that the report should not be read as a verdict on individual motives. That qualification did little to settle the matter. Indeed, by declining to rule out further scrutiny, the chair left open a possibility that a categorical denial would have closed. It would be tempting to infer that the panel had reached a private conclusion it was unwilling to publish. Yet the available evidence supports a narrower reading: the panel identified a pattern requiring explanation, while deliberately reserving judgement about why it had occurred.

The distinction matters. To infer misconduct from an omission alone is to move beyond the evidence; to treat the panel's language as entirely neutral is to ignore its rhetorical force. A defensible interpretation must account for both.

items.prompt: Explain the difference between what a statement entails and what it implicates.
items.modelAnswer: An entailment follows necessarily from the proposition, whereas an implicature is inferred from context and can usually be cancelled.

items.prompt: A public figure says, “I have nothing further to add at this stage.” Offer two plausible readings and explain what evidence would distinguish them.
items.modelAnswer: It could be a routine procedural response or a deliberate attempt to avoid commitment. Tone, prior questions and subsequent actions would help distinguish the readings.

items.prompt: Discuss whether hedging strengthens or weakens an argument in academic writing.
items.modelAnswer: Hedging can strengthen an argument by calibrating certainty to the evidence, though excessive qualification may obscure the writer's position.

items.prompt: Interpret the phrase “not entirely convincing” in a formal review. What criticism is being softened?
items.modelAnswer: The phrase signals substantial reservations while avoiding a blunt dismissal; the degree of criticism depends on the surrounding evaluation.

items.prompt: Explain how irony can reverse the apparent meaning of praise.
items.modelAnswer: Irony depends on a mismatch between literal wording and contextual cues such as tone, shared knowledge and the surrounding discourse.

items.prompt: Challenge an interlocutor who treats an omission as proof of deliberate deception.
items.modelAnswer: An omission may warrant scrutiny, but intent cannot be established from absence alone; alternative explanations need to be considered.

items.prompt: Compare “I disagree” with “I am not wholly persuaded”. What differences in stance and register do you hear?
items.modelAnswer: The first is direct and categorical; the second is more measured, leaves room for discussion and is common in formal debate.

items.prompt: Give an example of a presupposition and show how a speaker might challenge it.
items.modelAnswer: “When did you stop overlooking the evidence?” presupposes that the person previously overlooked it; one can reject the premise before answering.

items.prompt: Summarise a complex position while preserving its reservations and concessions.
items.modelAnswer: A good summary retains the main claim, the evidence offered, the limitations acknowledged and the concessions made, without turning a qualified position into certainty.

items.prompt: Reflect on a time when you misunderstood someone's implied meaning. Explain what contextual cue you overlooked.
items.modelAnswer: A strong response identifies the literal wording, the contextual cue missed, the original inference and how later evidence changed the interpretation.

content.audioTranscript: The spokesperson said the proposal was not without merit, but declined to endorse it. She added that the figures were preliminary and that no firm conclusion could yet be drawn. Asked whether the delay was deliberate, she said only that the timetable had been kept under review. The wording was cautious, and the omissions were conspicuous.
